name: The Ben Franklin Effect
statement: Doing someone a favour makes you like them more, not the other way round.
statementAccent: makes you like them more, not the other way round
meaning: The Ben Franklin effect is a psychological phenomenon in which a person who has done someone a favour is more likely to do that person another favour than if they had received a favour from them. Put plainly, doing someone a kindness makes you like them more, which is the reverse of the intuitive assumption that we do favours for people we already like. The effect is named after Benjamin Franklin, who in his autobiography described winning over a hostile fellow legislator by asking to borrow a rare book from him. After the rival lent the book, he became notably friendlier, and the two remained friends for life. Franklin quoted an old maxim to explain it: he that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than he whom you yourself have obliged. The effect is a striking case of attitudes following behaviour rather than the reverse.
mechanism: The usual explanation is cognitive dissonance. When you do a favour for someone you dislike or feel neutral toward, your action clashes with your attitude, creating an uncomfortable inconsistency: why would I help someone I do not care for. To resolve the dissonance, the mind adjusts the attitude to fit the behaviour, concluding that you must actually like or value the person, since you helped them. In this way the favour justifies itself after the fact, and liking increases to match the helpful act. The effect thus illustrates that behaviour can drive attitude change, a theme shared with self-perception theory, on which we infer our attitudes partly from observing our own actions. In a 1969 experiment by Jecker and Landy, participants who had won money were, in one condition, asked by the researcher to return it as a personal favour; those asked directly rated the researcher more favourably than those not asked, consistent with the effect.

examples.text: Franklin asked a rival legislator to lend him a rare book; having done the favour, the rival became friendly, and they remained friends thereafter.
In a 1969 study, people asked directly to return prize money as a personal favour rated the requester more favourably than those not asked.
The companion phenomenon is that people come to dislike or devalue those they have harmed, adjusting attitudes to justify the mistreatment.

variants.name: The dissonance account
variants.text: The explanation that doing a favour for a disliked person creates dissonance, resolved by revising one's attitude to like the person more.

variants.name: The harm counterpart
variants.text: The reverse effect in which harming someone leads one to devalue or dehumanise them, justifying the harm by lowering one's regard for the victim.

whyItMatters: The Ben Franklin effect is a classic demonstration that attitudes often follow actions rather than precede them, a central insight of cognitive dissonance and self-perception theory. It overturns the commonsense picture in which we help those we like, showing instead that helping can be a cause of liking, with practical implications for building rapport and relationships: asking someone for a small favour can, counterintuitively, warm them toward you. Its companion, the tendency to devalue those we harm, illuminates how people rationalise mistreatment and how cycles of hostility can deepen. Together these effects show the mind working to keep attitudes and behaviour consistent, adjusting feelings to fit what we have done. The phenomenon remains a memorable and widely cited example in social psychology of how our own actions shape whom we come to like and dislike.

working.text: perform a kindness for a person you do not particularly like, such as lending help or granting a request.
notice the clash between helping and your neutral or negative attitude toward the person.
resolve the inconsistency by coming to see the person more favourably, so liking rises to justify the favour.

limits: The Ben Franklin effect is a real but bounded phenomenon whose strength depends on circumstances; not every favour reliably increases liking, and factors like the size of the favour, whether it feels freely given or coerced, and the existing relationship all matter. The dissonance and self-perception explanations are well supported but the effect can be swamped by strong prior attitudes or by favours that feel manipulative. The Jecker and Landy study used a more complex design than a simple asked-versus-not comparison, and much of the evidence comes from particular experimental settings. So while the counterintuitive core, that doing a favour can raise liking, is well established, its magnitude and reliability vary, and it should be understood as a tendency rather than a guaranteed outcome.
misreadings: The effect is not that people who like you do you favours, which is the ordinary assumption; it is the reverse, that doing a favour increases liking. It does not mean any favour always produces affection, since coerced or manipulative-seeming favours may not, and strong prior dislike can persist. And Franklin's anecdote is an illustration, not proof; the empirical support comes from studies like Jecker and Landy, whose actual design was more nuanced than a simple two-group comparison, so treating the borrowed-book story as the whole basis of the effect understates the research behind it.
origin: Named after Benjamin Franklin, who described the phenomenon in his autobiography via the borrowed-book anecdote, and studied experimentally by Jecker and Landy in 1969; usually explained by cognitive dissonance.
